papers.title_in_file: Fourier series weight in quantum machine learning
papers.version_note: arXiv:2302.00105v2 [quant-ph], 26 Feb 2024 (the file name says 2023; the text layer is the 2024 version 2). Single copy of the paper in the text layer; references included.
papers.what_it_is: A QML paper that models a data-re-uploading variational circuit as a partial Fourier series and tests it in simulation (Pennylane) on trigonometric interpolation, binary and multiclass classification and a Hamiltonian-simulation style example.

existing.note: Right as stored. Two limits found later: the greater-than-92% accuracies appear only in the two-qubit table (the one-qubit table tops out well below), and no train/test split, repeat count or error bar is stated for any accuracy.
existing.value: The authors report some classifiers with accuracy greater than 92%, for example 92.5% on a two-circle task and 92.2% on a square task.
existing.anchor: Sec. VIII, Discussions, p.11; Fig. 13 caption, p.9
quotes: we have managed to have some classifiers with accuracy greater than 92%
we are talking about 92.5% accuracy
an accuracy of 92.2%
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with no stated split or repeats.
existing.reader_inference: Table I lists 92.10, 92.60, 92.50 and 92.20 for the two-qubit classifier at six, seven, eight and ten layers; the figure-13 values 92.5 and 92.2 match the eight- and ten-layer rows, which suggests they are one run each. The text does not say whether they are training or test accuracy.

existing.note: Right as stored. The paper elsewhere calls the demonstration of this intuition not trivial (Sec. VIII), which is held as a separate stated-limit assertion.
existing.value: The authors state that their results conclude that one can strongly consider the quantum computer a Fourier series.
quotes: The results conclude that we can strongly consider the quantum computer a Fourier series.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the paper's Fourier-series derivation is adapted from cited work and the coefficients are only approximated.
existing.reader_inference: The claim rests on a model class of re-uploading circuits with rotation-gate encoding, not on every quantum computer; the wording is broader than the setup.

existing.note: Right as stored. Sec. IV.E states it; the Conclusion adds a separate limit (highest-frequency inputs), held as its own assertion.
existing.value: The authors state that the qubits' scarcity and susceptibility to errors and decoherence significantly cap the complexity and size of the models they can reliably implement.
quotes: The qubits' scarcity and susceptibility to errors and decoherence significantly cap the complexity and size of the models we can reliably implement.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states this as a limit of its own framework in Sec. IV.E.

assertions.value: The authors state that they defined a quantum variational feature map together with a quantum variational circuit, which they say can behave like a proper quantum neural network, and that they use it to check the Fourier series weight in such models.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V.A, Our quantum model, p.5; Fig. 3 caption
quotes: we have defined a quantum variational Feature Map together with a quantum variational circuit that, taking advantage of its mixture, can behave like a proper quantum neural network
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own model in Sec. V.A (equation 8 and Fig. 3).
assertions.reader_inference: The model is a data re-uploading circuit of the kind in the cited Perez-Salinas and Schuld et al. work; the paper's own addition is the variational feature map.

assertions.value: The authors state that this work follows the data encoding Hamiltonians idea for loading classical data.
quotes: This work follows the data encoding Hamiltonians idea
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own encoding choice in Sec. IV.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that the article deals exclusively with classical data: a quantum computer processes the classical data and returns the outcome after measurement.
quotes: This article deals exclusively with classical data;
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Sec. IV.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that they performed and tested all the proposed models using the Pennylane framework.
quotes: We performed and tested all the proposed models using the Pennylane framework.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in the abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper names no hardware device and no noise model, and its limitations section speaks of hardware in general terms, so the results read as noiseless simulation; the text does not say so outright.

assertions.value: The authors state that in their case they use the computational basis Z as the observable.
quotes: In our case, we use the computational basis Z.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own measurement setup in Sec. IV.D.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to test the classifier, they generated four datasets named crown, circle, square and SWP.
quotes: we have generated four datasets (crown, circle, square, SWP
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own classifier test sets in Sec. VII.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The ethics statement says no new data were created or analyzed, which does not fit synthetic datasets generated for the study; the dataset sizes and split are not stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to test the trigonometric interpolation model, they use the sine, cosine, log, saw-tooth and square functions as the input signal.
quotes: To test it, we operate as the input signal, the function sine, cosine, log, saw-tooth, and square.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own interpolation test set in Sec. VII.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that equation (19) is a partial multivariate Fourier series, with the accessible frequencies entirely determined by the spectra of the coding Hamiltonians and the Fourier coefficients determined by the unitary estimates.
assertions.anchor: Sec. VI, Fourier series based on quantum circuit, p.6
quotes: The equation (19) is, in fact, a partial multivariate Fourier series, with the accessible frequencies entirely determined by the spectra of the coding Hamiltonians Hk and the Fourier coefficients determined by the unitary estimates.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result adapted from the cited Schuld, Sweke and Meyer work; the paper states it without a theorem statement of its own.
assertions.reader_inference: The section says it recovers and adapts that cited work ('we recover the work [16]'), and it considers one layer and absorbs the trainable blocks into the state and observable, so the form is for a simplified model.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from Section VI, they can assume that f(x) has a Fourier series decomposition.
assertions.anchor: Sec. VI.1, Our model as a trigonometric interpolation, p.6
quotes: From the section (VI) we can assume that f (x) has Fourier series decomposition.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as the assumption its interpolation analysis starts from.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Fourier series converges faster for smoother functions, per equation (25).
quotes: The Fourier series converges faster for smoother functions (equation (25))
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook fact given without proof or a citation of its own in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: This is classical Fourier analysis, not a result about the quantum model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of data loadings, the circuit depth, the layers or the repetitions are proportional to the degree of the function to be interpolated.
quotes: is proportional to the degree of the function to be interpolated.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with no derivation or measurement in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: In the cited expressivity work the number of accessible frequencies grows with the number of data encodings; this paper does not prove it.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to validate the model on Hamiltonian time evolution, their aim was simulating p(x) = cos(tx) and g(x) = sin(tx) for some instant t.
quotes: Thus our aim was simulating p(x) = cos(tx) and g(x) = sin(tx) for some instant t.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own Hamiltonian-simulation test in Sec. VI.2.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the sine and cosine fitting also shown in Fig. 8; no Hamiltonian larger than a scalar phase is simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that they define the sample rate frequency to meet the Nyquist theorem.
quotes: We define sample rate frequency to accomplish a Nyquist theorem
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own sampling setup in Sec. VII.1.

assertions.value: The authors report four tests with a 20Hz square signal at different numbers of layers and samples, and state that with more high-frequency components the reconstruction of the squared signal is achieved, with the Gibbs phenomenon observable.
assertions.anchor: Fig. 6 caption, Sec. VII.1, p.8; the layer counts and sample counts are in the caption
quotes: four tests with the square signal of 20Hz with the different number of layers (L) and sample (n)
With more high-frequency components, the reconstruction of the squared signal is achieved.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study, reported through figures only.
assertions.reader_inference: The caption lists three layers with twenty samples, then twenty and thirty layers with one hundred samples; the paper gives no error figure for the fits.

assertions.value: The authors report four tests with a 20Hz sawtooth signal at different numbers of layers and samples, again studying harmonic decomposition and the Gibbs phenomenon.
quotes: four tests with the sawtooth signal of 20Hz with the different number of layers (L) and sample (n)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study, reported through figures only.
assertions.reader_inference: The Fig. 7 caption repeats the Fig. 6 caption word for word, including 'squared signal', so it is probably a copy and its description of the sawtooth results is not independent.

assertions.value: The authors report fits of sine and cosine input signals at several frequencies and with amplitude modulation, and state that they realized the model limitation on the highest-frequency input signal.
quotes: We realized the model limitation on the highest-frequency input signal.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation from figures in one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors report, from an amplitude-modulation experiment multiplying two quite different frequency sines, that the tail of the signal is seen to decay and the number of repetitions (layers) must be increased considerably to solve it.
assertions.anchor: Fig. 14 caption, p.11; Sec. VIII, p.11; Sec. IX Conclusion, p.11
quotes: The tail of the signal is seen to decay, and we must considerably increase the number of repetitions (layers) to solve it.
we have also detected some limitations in better adapting the model to the highest-frequency input signals.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as a limit of its own model in Sec. VIII and Sec. IX.
assertions.reader_inference: The limit is stated qualitatively; no frequency, layer count or error value is given for the failure.

assertions.value: The authors report a Fourier coefficient plot for a 3Hz sinusoidal input signal, sampled above the Nyquist frequency at 120Hz, with 12 repetitions, computed with the Pennylane Fourier tooling.
quotes: the case of a 3Hz sinusoidal input signal, sampled above the Nyquist frequency at 120Hz, and with 12 repetitions
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation, shown only as a plot.
assertions.reader_inference: The caption says the coefficients are 'potentially, in this case, rather real than imagined' and gives no numeric coefficient values or error.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to calculate the Fourier coefficients of the quantum model, they relied on an approximation and classical computation with the fft (their figure 10), and that calculating the coefficients is very challenging.
assertions.anchor: Sec. VIII, p.10; Fig. 10 caption, p.9
quotes: In this paper, we have relied on an approximation and classical with the fft to calculate them (see figure (10)).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own coefficient method in Sec. VIII.
assertions.reader_inference: The coefficients are therefore estimated classically from sampled outputs of the model, which is a numerical check rather than a closed-form derivation; the paper later calls this method 'groundbreaking'.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains a challenge to finish determining with greater precision the Fourier coefficients.
quotes: Also, it remains a challenge to finish determining with greater precision the Fourier coefficients.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open problem in Sec. IX.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although intuition leads them to think the quantum model is a Fourier series because the ansatz gates are rotation gates, the demonstration of this intuition is not trivial.
quotes: Although intuition leads us to think that the quantum model is a Fourier series
the demonstration of this intuition is not trivial.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as a limit of its own argument in Sec. VIII.
assertions.reader_inference: This sits in tension with the Conclusion's 'strongly consider the quantum computer a Fourier series' and with the Conclusion's 'demonstrated'.

assertions.value: The authors state that they have confirmed that the proposed model is a partial Fourier series and that it can be used for trigonometric interpolation.
quotes: We have confirmed that the proposed model is a partial Fourier series.
The model can
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the support is the cited derivation plus interpolation plots, with no quantitative fit error.

assertions.value: The paper tabulates classifier accuracy against the number of layers and parameters for a quantum neural classifier with one qubit and for one with two qubits.
assertions.anchor: Table I (one qubit and two qubits) and Table II captions, p.10; accuracies run from 52.60 to 73.91 for one qubit at one to ten layers and from 48.90 to 92.60 for two qubits
quotes: Quantum neural classifier (1 qubit)
Quantum neural classifier (2 qubits)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the figures are in the tables.
assertions.reader_inference: The one-qubit table lists 52.60, 59.90, 62.60, 66.61, 63.72, 68.85, 67.91, 67.20 and 73.91 for 1 to 8 and 10 layers; the two-qubit table lists 48.90, 70.30, 84.5, 84.90, 87.50, 92.10, 92.60, 92.50 and 92.20, so accuracy rises with layers and then flattens near 92 to 93 for two qubits. Both table captions say the study is the two-qubit binary classifier, so they are inconsistent with their headings. No repeats, split or baseline is given.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Social Workers' Problem (SWP) was solved with the quantum neural classifier, tabulating accuracy for several combinations of patients and social workers (Table III).
assertions.anchor: Table III, p.10; Sec. VIII; accuracy falls from 70.3 for three patients and two social workers to 47.2 for five patients and four social workers, all at two layers
quotes: The SWP leveraged the quantum neural classifier.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the figures are in the table.
assertions.reader_inference: Table III shows 70.3, 63.2, 57.7, 48.1 and 47.2 as the instance grows from three patients and two workers to five and four; accuracy falls as the instance grows, and the paper does not comment on this or give a classical baseline.

assertions.value: The authors state that going from a binary classifier to a multiclass one is costly, and that one must run (n + 1)n/2 quantum models.
quotes: it is costly to go from binary classifier to multiclass; one must run (n + 1)n/2 quantum models.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with no derivation; no multiclass result is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: A one-versus-one scheme needs n(n-1)/2 models and one-versus-rest needs n, so (n+1)n/2 matches neither; the paper does not define n here. Sec. VI.3 elsewhere describes a multiclass circuit that reads one qubit, with no results shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the binary classifier of their figure (4) they measure the expected value of the circuit and take the sign of the output.
assertions.anchor: Sec. VI.3, Our model as a classifier, p.7
quotes: In the case of the binary classifier given by the figure (4), we measure the expected value of the proposed quantum circuit, and after the measurement, we make the sign of the output.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own classifier readout in Sec. VI.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CNOT gates used to interleave the data, so that only the first qubit is read, allow them to reduce the effect of the barren plateau in the case of a classifier.
assertions.anchor: Fig. 5 caption, p.7; Sec. VI.3, p.7
quotes: This allows us to reduce the effect of the barren plateau in the case of a classifier.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper reports no gradient-variance or training measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: Reading a single qubit gives a local cost, which the cited barren-plateau literature links to milder gradient decay; this paper does not test it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the typical design, with a single fixed feature map at the start of the circuit and no repetition, does not help the quantum model generalize the parameterized function better, as a neural network does.
quotes: Said design/strategy does not help the quantum model generalize the parameterized function better as a neural network
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim, with no experiment in the paper comparing a single embedding to repeated data loading.
assertions.reader_inference: The Fig. 4 caption makes the related claim that without reloading the data a circuit learns only a sine or cosine; no single-embedding baseline is run.

assertions.value: The authors state that without repeating the layer and reloading the data x, their one-qubit circuit will only learn a sine or cosine function.
quotes: Without repeating the layer and reloading the data x, this circuit will only learn a sine or cosine function.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement in a figure caption, not tested separately.
assertions.reader_inference: This follows from the single-frequency spectrum of one encoding gate in the cited Schuld et al. analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that their feature map determines the frequencies and the variational quantum circuit determines the coefficients of the Fourier series.
quotes: Our Feature Map, which implements our data encoding strategy, determines the frequencies ω, and our variational quantum circuit determines the coefficients cω.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement from the cited Fourier-expressivity framework, given in captions without proof here.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in case of a volume of data that presents a trigonometric distribution, the proposed model will be able to speed up the hyperparameter optimization process.
quotes: in case of a volume of data that presents a trigonometric distribution, the proposed model will be able to speed up the hyperparameter optimization process.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no experiment or analysis in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states just before this that it has made no detailed study of computational complexity, and shows no hyperparameter search run.

assertions.value: The authors state that they have not made a detailed study of the algorithm's computational complexity.
quotes: We have not made a detailed study of the algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as a limit of its own work in Sec. VIII.
assertions.reader_inference: Statements of speed-up and of scalability elsewhere in the paper (Sec. V.B, Sec. VIII) therefore have no complexity analysis behind them.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by leveraging efficient quantum circuit designs and optimizing qubit usage, they ensure that the model remains computationally feasible even as the number of qubits grows.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V.B, Scalability and adaptability, p.5
quotes: we ensure that our model remains computationally feasible even as the number of qubits grows.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no scaling experiment or analysis in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The circuits shown have one qubit (Fig. 4) and three qubits (Fig. 5), and the tables use one and two qubits; no experiment varies qubit count to test scaling.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scalability of quantum hardware remains a paramount challenge, and that the optimal design of quantum algorithms that fully leverage the theoretical capabilities of quantum computing remains an area of ongoing research.
quotes: the scalability of quantum hardware remains a paramount challenge
remains an area of ongoing research.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these as limits of its framework in Sec. IV.E.

assertions.value: The authors state, for their dataset figure, that the model allows them to better interpolate the data from the dataset, and that one possible application is to find a continuous parameterized function from discrete data.
quotes: We can observe how the model allows us to better interpolate the data from the dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author reading of a figure with no baseline or error measure stated.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Better' is relative to nothing the text names; the dataset is not described.

assertions.value: The authors state that equation (5) helps to analyze the training errors of the quantum model.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV.C, The error calculation, p.4; Fig. 12 caption, p.9
quotes: Equation (5) helps to analyze the training errors.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own error measure in Sec. IV.C.
assertions.reader_inference: Equation (5) is a mean of squared differences between model output and label; Sec. VI.3 gives the classifier a different cost, a distance between states, so the paper uses two cost definitions.

assertions.value: The authors state that in this paper they have experimented with and demonstrated the weight of the Fourier series in quantum machine learning.
quotes: In this paper, we have experimented with and demonstrated the weight of the Fourier series in quantum machine learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own conclusion, not tested apart from the reported simulations.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Weight' is not defined or measured as a quantity; the support is the interpolation plots and classifier tables.

assertions.value: The authors state that they introduce a groundbreaking methodology for calculating Fourier coefficients, adapted for classification and trigonometric interpolation scenarios.
quotes: We introduce a groundbreaking methodology for calculating Fourier coefficients
assertions.certainty_reason: A self-assessment by the authors with no comparison to other methods.
assertions.reader_inference: The method in Fig. 10 is an FFT of sampled model outputs, as the same section says; the novelty claim is unsupported by any comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that the code to reproduce the figures and explore settings of the model is in a GitHub repository, pifparfait/Fourier_Based_QML.
quotes: The reader can find the code in the following GitHub repository
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states where its code is held.
assertions.reader_inference: The URL is split by a line break in the text layer; the repository was not opened.
